lead: A rotary inductive device turns shaft angle into an AC voltage. One winding sits on the stator, one on the rotor, and the mutual inductance between them changes as the shaft turns, so the induced voltage carries the angle in its amplitude and phase. Three devices use this idea: the induction potentiometer, the synchro pair and the microsyn. Only the microsyn is truly brushless, because its rotor carries no winding. The other two reach their rotor winding through slip rings. Their gain over a resistive potentiometer is no sliding contact and no wiper noise. Uses: radar antenna pointing, valve position feedback, AC servo error detection.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for mutual inductance and Chapter 3.2 for amplitude-plus-phase output.

sections.h3: The common idea: angle sets the coupling

blocks.text: Most of these devices put one winding on the stator and one on the rotor that follows the shaft. The excitation drives one winding; its flux crosses the air gap and links the other. The strength of that link is the mutual inductance M, in henry (H). Turning the shaft changes M smoothly: M = M_max cos θ, where M_max is the peak mutual inductance and θ is the shaft angle measured from maximum coupling.

By Faraday's law the output is an AC voltage at the excitation frequency f, with amplitude proportional to M and therefore to cos θ. When θ passes the null, M changes sign and the output flips 180° in phase. Amplitude gives the size of the angle, phase gives the side of the null.
The output is a carrier: a fixed-frequency AC wave whose envelope follows the shaft. A phase-sensitive demodulator turns it into a signed DC voltage. Keep f well above the fastest shaft motion.

An induction potentiometer is a rotary transformer with a distributed winding. The stator winding is spread over many slots, so its mutual inductance to the rotor winding varies smoothly with angle instead of in steps. The rotor carries a single winding, fed through slip rings, and the output is taken from the stator. Nothing slides on a resistance track.

blocks.where: e_o is the output rms voltage (V); k is the coupling constant, less than 1; E_x is the rms excitation voltage (V); θ is the shaft angle from electrical zero.

blocks.text: Here θ is measured from electrical zero, the position of minimum coupling, so the cos becomes a sin. The sine is linear only near the null, where sin θ ≈ θ with θ in radians. A few tens of degrees is the usual working range; beyond that the scale factor falls away. Full 360° measurement needs a resolver or a two-speed arrangement.

At the null the output is not exactly zero. Winding imperfections and space harmonics leave a residual called the null voltage, typically a few millivolts, and it sets the smallest angle the device can resolve. Against a resistive potentiometer: no sliding contact, no wear, no contact noise, but you need AC excitation and demodulation, and the range is limited. Typical uses are valve stem position and slow remote angle indication.

A synchro transmitter has a single-phase rotor on the shaft and a three-phase stator: three identical windings spaced 120° electrical. The rotor is excited. Each stator phase is coupled to the rotor axis at its own angle, so the three phase voltages are K·E_r·cos θ, K·E_r·cos(θ − 120°) and K·E_r·cos(θ + 120°), where E_r is the rotor excitation (V rms), θ is the rotor angle and K is a constant. The three voltages together fix θ over the full 360°.

The control transformer looks the same but works in reverse. Its three-phase stator is wired to the transmitter's stator, so it receives the same flux pattern; its single-phase rotor is the output. With zero set at θ_R = θ_T, the rotor voltage is e = E_max·sin Δθ, where E_max is the output at 90° error (V rms), θ_R is the control transformer rotor angle and θ_T is the transmitter rotor angle.

Near the null sin Δθ ≈ Δθ in radians, so the output measures the error directly, and its phase against the excitation says which way the error lies. Feed it to a servo amplifier and the motor turns until Δθ = 0. This is the standard error detector of an AC position servo, used in radar antenna pointing and valve positioners.

The two units are not interchangeable. The transmitter rotor is a low-impedance primary that must hold flux constant; the control transformer rotor is a high-impedance secondary built to give a small, clean null.

A microsyn is a compact, sensitive version. The stator and a passive rotor both carry fine teeth separated by a very small air gap. Four stator windings are connected as a bridge: two excited, two giving the output. At the null the teeth align and the bridge balances; a small rotation spoils the alignment and unbalances the bridge, so a tiny angle gives a large output. The rotor has no winding, so no slip rings are needed. Microsyns appear in gyro pick-offs and precision instruments.

blocks.text: All three devices share the same practical checks: linearity near the null, size of the null voltage, excitation frequency and phase. A low-resistance load pulls the flux down and shifts both the scale factor and the null.

figure.caption: The three rotary inductive devices. Only the synchro pair gives an error signal between two shafts, because a transmitter is compared with a control transformer.

spec.aria: Tree of rotary inductive devices: induction potentiometer, synchro with its transmitter and control transformer, and microsyn.

example.question: A synchro transmitter rotor is at θ_T = 30°. The control transformer rotor is at θ_R = 40°. The excitation is 26 V rms and the control transformer gives 10 V rms at 90° error. Find the error angle and the control transformer output. Which way should the servo turn?
steps: Control transformer relation: e = E_max·sin Δθ, with E_max = 10 V rms, the output at 90° error.
Cross-check: Δθ = 10° = 0.1745 rad, so E_max·Δθ = 1.745 V rms; the two agree within 0.5%.
The 26 V excitation only sets the scale; E_max already includes it. The sign is positive because θ_R > θ_T.
The servo must reduce Δθ to zero, so it turns the control transformer rotor from 40° towards 30°.
example.answer: Δθ = 10° and the output is 1.74 V rms; the servo turns the rotor so that θ_R falls from 40° to 30°.
example.check:
import math
theta_T = 30.0
theta_R = 40.0
E_max = 10.0
dtheta = theta_R - theta_T
e_out = E_max * math.sin(math.radians(dtheta))
linear = E_max * math.radians(dtheta)
print(round(dtheta, 2))
print(round(e_out, 2))
print(round(linear, 3))

example.question: An induction potentiometer has excitation E_x = 10 V rms and coupling constant k = 0.5. Find the output at θ = 30°, and say what the null voltage means.
steps: The null voltage is the small residual still present at θ = 0 because of winding imperfections and harmonics; this formula does not give it.
example.answer: The output is 2.5 V rms at θ = 30°; the null voltage is a separate small residual at θ = 0.
example.check:
import math
k = 0.5
E_x = 10.0
theta = 30.0
print(round(k * E_x * math.sin(math.radians(theta)), 2))

traps: Using degrees in E_max·Δθ. The sine form accepts degrees, but the linear form needs radians.
Assuming the control transformer output is proportional to Δθ itself. At 10° the sine is 0.174, not 0.10.
Treating a synchro transmitter and a control transformer as interchangeable. Their rotor windings are designed for opposite roles.
Reading only the magnitude. Without phase you cannot tell which side of the null the error lies on.
Confusing the induction potentiometer (one output winding, cannot separate θ from 180° − θ) with the synchro transmitter (three stator voltages fix the angle over 360°).

quiz.q: How are the windings of a synchro transmitter arranged?
quiz.a: A single-phase rotor on the shaft, excited from an AC supply, and a three-phase stator whose three identical windings are spaced 120° electrical apart.

quiz.q: Why does the output phase, not just the amplitude, carry information in a rotary inductive device?
quiz.a: The induced voltage is e = −jωMi, so its amplitude follows M and its sign follows the sign of M. When the shaft crosses the null, M reverses and the output flips 180°. Amplitude gives the size of the angle, phase gives the side.

quiz.q: A control transformer gives 10 V rms at 90° error. Find its output at an error of 4°.
quiz.a: e = E_max·sin Δθ = 10 × sin 4° = 10 × 0.06976 = 0.698 V rms, about 0.70 V rms. The small-angle check, 10 × 0.0698 rad, agrees.

quiz.q: An induction potentiometer with k = 0.4 and E_x = 8 V rms is set at θ = 60°. Find the output.
Why is a control transformer used only near the null, and not over a wide angle?
quiz.a: The output is E_max·sin Δθ. At 30° error the sine is 0.500 while Δθ in radians is 0.524, an error of about 5%, and the gap grows with angle. At 90° the output peaks, and beyond 90° it falls although the error is larger, so the magnitude becomes ambiguous and only the phase still tells the direction.
The small residual output still present at electrical zero, caused by winding imperfections and space harmonics. It is typically a few millivolts and sets the resolution.

quiz.q: Why does a microsyn not need slip rings?
quiz.a: Its rotor is a passive toothed iron piece with no winding, so no connection has to reach the rotating part. Rotation changes the tooth alignment and hence the coupling of the stator windings, which are all fixed.

quiz.q: A student replaces a faulty synchro transmitter with a control transformer of the same size. Why does the system fail?
quiz.a: The transmitter rotor is a low-impedance excited primary that must hold the flux constant and drive three stator lines. The control transformer rotor is a high-impedance output secondary designed for a small null. Swapping them gives the wrong scale factor, a poor null and incorrect loading of the stator lines.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry still uses synchros in aircraft and legacy radar, where a synchro-to-digital converter chip turns the three line voltages into a digital angle. In new designs the resolver, a close relative with two stator windings at 90°, has largely replaced the synchro, and optical encoders replace both where absolute digital position is wanted. Toothed microsyn-type structures reappear in MEMS gyroscopes and in variable-reluctance resolvers.
